# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

The answer to the first point is clear. There is no doubt that, just as men can kill by God’s permission, so too can they truly and really remove that member or another. But in such cases, the demons do not act through the witches of whom mention is now being made. By these points, the solution to the second argument is also clear. But the claim that because God allows the generative power to be bewitched for certain reasons, it must therefore be allowed that such a member be truly and really removed, is invalid. It does not follow that this always happens, for such an event would not occur by way of witchcraft, nor do witches intend this when they perform such works, because they do not have the power to restore the member when they wish and know how. From this it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by <term>prestigiosa arte</term> <gloss>illusory or deceptive art</gloss>.

Regarding the third point concerning the wife of Lot, we say: her conversion was true and not by illusory art; however, we are now speaking of illusory art.

To the fourth point, that demons can induce some substantial forms and therefore can also remove them: it is said, with regard to the magicians of Pharaoh, that they produced true serpents. Demons can indeed produce certain effects around imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do regarding humans, for whom God has greater care. This is according to the text: "Is God concerned about oxen?" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:9</note>. Nevertheless, as has been said, they can always, by God’s permission, harm humans truly and realistically, or even by illusory art. By these points, the solution to the final argument is also clear.

<margin>
# Question 10. Whether witches work upon men by transforming them into beastly forms through illusory art.
</margin>

Fourth, the truth itself is clarified, where it is also said that they transform men into beasts. Concerning how this happens, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. From the 26th Question, 5th Chapter, *Episcopi*, from the Council of Anquira: "Whoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or the worse, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is undoubtedly an infidel and worse than a pagan." And let us use the arguments of Saint Thomas in the second book of his *Sentences*, distinction 8, "Whether demons can impress themselves upon the bodily senses by deluding them with illusions." Where, first, he argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must be somewhere, yet it cannot be only in the sense, because the sense does not have any species except that which is received from things, and there is no true beast there according to the canon law cited. Nor, again, can it be in the thing that is seen, such as when a woman appears to be a beast, because two substantial forms cannot exist in the same subject at once and simultaneously. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen cannot be anywhere, no illusory deception can occur in the eye of the one seeing, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form.

Furthermore, if it is said that that form is in the surrounding air, this cannot be; both because air is not receptive to any form or figure, and also because one and the same air cannot always remain around that person due to its fluidity, especially when they are moving. Furthermore, if this were the case, such a transformation would be seen by everyone, which does not happen, because demons are not seen to deceive the visions of holy men, at least. Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportionate to it. However, the active thing proportionate to the sense is twofold: one as if originating the act, namely the object; the other as if conveying it, such as the medium. But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor the medium conveying it. Regarding the first, that it cannot be the object: it cannot be taken from any thing, as was touched upon in the previous argument, since it is not in the sense as received from a thing, nor in the thing itself, nor in the air as a conveying medium, as was touched upon in the third argument. Furthermore, if a demon moves the internal cognitive faculty, either he does this by presenting himself...

<summary>This page concludes the refutation of arguments regarding the reality of demonic "transformation" of human limbs and beastly forms, asserting that such phenomena are not physical realities but illusory deceptions, while citing canonical authorities and Saint Thomas Aquinas to define the limits of demonic power.</summary>
<keywords>witchcraft, illusory art, demonic illusion, substantial forms, Saint Thomas Aquinas, Council of Anquira, visual perception, canon law</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...The gods themselves give warning and command that He be worshipped everywhere. But the unlearned and those of impious nature, to whom fate has not truly granted the reception of gifts from the gods, nor the understanding of the immortal Jupiter, do not heed both the gods and divine men; they have rejected all the gods indeed, but they have chosen not only to follow no hatreds toward the forbidden demons, but even to revere them. Yet, while pretending to worship God, they do not perform the very things through which God is adored. For God, as the Father of all, is in need of nothing; but it is well for us when we adore Him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to Him through imitation and the inquiry of Him. For inquiry, he says, purges; imitation deifies by working an affection toward Him. He has indeed preached well that God is the Father and has spoken of the virtues by which He must be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, whether the life of the holy is praised or blamed. But it was only in Christians—or rather, it is slandered as much as the demons, whom he deems gods, desire—as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what base things and what dishonors were performed in the theaters and temples for the sake of the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God, and from this to understand where there is an edifice and where a ruin of morals. Who, moreover, told this to him or inspired him, if not a diabolical spirit, such a vain and open lie: that Christians revere rather than hate the demons whom the Hebrews were forbidden to worship? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped also forbids sacrificing to the celestial, holy angels and virtues of God—whom we venerate and love as most blessed fellow citizens in this mortal pilgrimage of ours—thundering in His law which He gave to His Hebrew people; and He brought it in very menacingly, saying: "He who sacrifices to the gods will be eradicated." And lest anyone should think it was commanded that one should not sacrifice to the wicked, earthly spirits—whom this man calls the "least" or "lesser"—because they are also called gods in the holy scriptures, they are not [called gods] of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations, which the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint</note> clearly placed in the Psalm, saying: "For all the gods of the nations are demons." Lest anyone, therefore, think that while it is forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, it is permitted to sacrifice to the celestial ones—either to all or to some—He immediately added: "Except to the Lord alone," that is, except to the Lord only, lest by chance someone think that the "Lord alone" refers to the sun god, to whom he thinks sacrifice should be made. That this is not to be understood in this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom such a great man and even this philosopher bears witness, gave a law to His Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language—not obscure and unknown, but now spread among all nations—in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to the gods will be eradicated, unless to the Lord only." What need is there in this law of His and in His prophets to investigate many things about this matter? Or rather, not to investigate, for they are not abstruse or rare, but to collect the open and frequent ones, and to place them in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that the true and supreme God wished to be sacrificed to by no one at all except Himself alone. Behold, let this one thing, briefly—or rather, grandly and menacingly, but truthfully—spoken by that God whom their most learned men so excellently preach, be heard, be feared, be fulfilled, lest eradication follow the disobedient. "He who sacrifices to the gods will be eradicated," He says, "except to the Lord alone." Not that He is in need of any thing, but because it is profitable for us that we be His. For it is sung to Him in the sacred writings of the Hebrews: "I said to the Lord, You are my God, for You do not need my goods." The most illustrious and best sacrifice to Him, however, is ourselves. This is His city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our oblations, which are known to the faithful, just as we have argued in the preceding books. For the oracles thundered through the Hebrew prophets that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of things to come were going to cease, and that the nations would offer one sacrifice from the rising of the sun to the setting, just as we now see happening.

<summary>Augustine argues that the Hebrew law, widely known and clear, forbids sacrifice to any but the one true God, refuting the idea that sacrifices to lesser spirits or celestial beings were ever permitted. He defines the true sacrifice as the self-offering of the faithful, which constitutes the City of God.</summary>
<keywords>Sacrifice, Hebrews, Demonology, Idolatry, Law of Moses, Christian worship, City of God, Porphyry</keywords>

and tell them: "I bear this willingly for your sake, oh Queen. You will restore me to wholeness, or at the very least, you alone are enough for me in place of all else." Cherish me with your loving heart alone, and in this way I shall not feel the losses of my reputation, nor even of my life.

*Sorrow.* I am torn apart everywhere in the public squares.

*Reason.* Take it in good part. The common people will make you known, virtue will make you illustrious, and a clear conscience will make you secure.

### Concerning shame over praise bestowed upon the unworthy.
## DIAL. XXVI.

> Praise with restraint, for when you praise wrongfully,
> Should you later condemn, it will be a mark of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.

<note>A large, ornamental initial L marks the start of the response.</note>

*Reason.* That which is evil often arises from a good root. For good and innocent people, such as they themselves are, imagine others to be the same. Hence they are even more prone to praise than they should be; and although I admit that it is wrong to praise the unworthy, it is nonetheless much worse to slander the innocent.

*Sorrow.* I have praised the unworthy.

*Reason.* If you did so knowingly, you are reprehensible; but if you did so in ignorance, you are excusable. It is less of an evil to be deceived than to deceive. For to be deceived is a stranger's act, but to deceive is the specific crime of the deceiver.

*Sorrow.* The praise of another contributes to my own infamy.

*Reason.* On the contrary, it is either your own fault or your own ignorance. For just as there is no praise in the actions of another, so too there is no infamy in them.

*Sorrow.* I grieve greatly for having praised the unworthy.

*Reason.* See to it, then, that you do not often have cause for this same grief. Beware of rushing rashly into praising or slandering. For there is a craving for both—and to speak properly—a disease and a certain itching of the tongue, which is restless and ignorant of quiet. Its bridle and restraint are numbered among the works of the highest perfection, as Scripture says:

<summary>In this dialogue, Reason consoles Sorrow regarding the dangers of uncritical praise, emphasizing that being deceived by the unworthy is a pardonable error while warning against the restless tongue.</summary>
<keywords>praise, slander, reputation, ignorance, conscience, virtue, restraint, speech</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...aid the purgations of women.</meta> and the application of its juice. Olympias of Thebes added hyssop and nitre. The ash of stag horn taken as a drink. Likewise for a laboring womb. Also, apply bull bile with opium, two obols in weight. It is beneficial to fumigate the womb with stag hair. They report that stags, when they sense they are pregnant, swallow a small stone, which is found in their excrement or in the womb (for it is also found there), and is guarded by being tied on. Small bones are also found in the heart and womb, which are very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. Regarding the pumice stone, which is found in the uterus of cows in a similar way, we have spoken in the nature of oxen. Applied wolf fat softens the womb. Its liver relieves their pains. Eating the meat of a wolf is beneficial for those about to give birth. Or if it is nearby when they begin to labor, it is effective, even against harmful applications. However, for it to arrive after the labor has begun is dangerous. The hare is also of great use to women. Its dried lung, taken as a drink, aids the womb. Its liver with Samian earth in water as a drink is for discharges. Its rennet is for the afterbirth. They avoid baths on the previous day. Also, applied with saffron and leek juice, and inserted in wool, it expels dead fetuses. If the wombs of hares are eaten, they believe it causes the conception of males. This is also achieved by their testicles and rennet. A fetus removed from a hare's uterus is said to bring lasting fertility to those who have ceased to bear children. But also, it is healthy before conception for the man to drink it. Likewise, nine grains of dung for a virgin so that her breasts may remain firm forever. Also with the rennet. For this reason, they smear it with honey where they do not want hair to grow back after it has been plucked. For inflation of the womb, apply boar or pig dung with oil. It stops discharges more effectively if it is flour of the dried substance or sprinkled in a potion, or if pregnant women or those who have just given birth are in pain. Drinking sow's milk with honeyed wine aids the labor of women. Taken by itself, it replenishes the failing milk of those who have just given birth. The same substance, when smeared on with the blood of a female pig, causes the breasts to grow less. If they ache, they are soothed by drinking ass's milk. Taken with added honey, it also aids their purgations. The aged tallow of the same animal also heals ulcerations of the womb, and when applied in wool, it softens the hardness of the womb. Used fresh or aged, applied with water, it has the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>hair-removing agent</gloss>. The aged spleen of the same animal, applied with water, increases the abundance of breast milk. Fumigation corrects the womb. Fumigated donkey hooves hasten labor, so as even to induce an abortion; it is not used in any other way than this, which kills the living fetus. If fresh dung of the same animal is applied, it is said to stop blood discharges remarkably well. Also, the ash of the same dung, which, when applied, is also beneficial to the womb. Horse foam applied for forty days before the first hairs appear causes them to cease. Likewise, a decoction of stag horn. It is better if the horns are fresh. The womb is washed and aided by mare's milk. If the fetus is felt to be dead, the spleen, drunk in sweet water, expels it. Likewise, fumigation with hooves or dried dung. Butter infused stops a prolapsed womb. Bull bile mixed with rose oil opens a hardened womb; apply it externally in wool with terebinth resin. They also say that by the fumigation of bull dung, prolapsed wombs are checked, and labor is aided. But conception is aided by drinking cow's milk. It is certain that sterility occurs because of the strain of labor. Olympias of Thebes affirms that this is corrected by bull bile, snake fat, and verdigris, added to honey, and applied to the affected areas before intercourse. Calf bile, if sprinkled on the womb during intercourse while purging, softens the hardness of the belly and reduces the discharge when the umbilical cord has been cut, and is entirely beneficial to the womb. They set the measure of the bile at the weight of a denarius mixed with a third of an ounce of celery and enough almond oil to seem sufficient, and they apply this in wool. Male calf bile is triturated with half its amount of honey and kept for the womb. If they eat calf meat roasted with birthwort <note>original: "aristolochia"</note> around the time of conception, they promise the birth of males. Calf marrow, boiled in wine and water with tallow, is beneficial for ulcerations of the womb. Likewise, fox fat and cat excrement applied with resin and rose oil. They consider it most useful to fumigate the womb with goat horn. The blood of wild goats with sea-palm removes hair. But the bile of other goats, when sprinkled, softens the callosity of the womb and causes conception after a purgation. The power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>hair-removing agent</gloss> is achieved in this way; it is kept applied for three days after the hairs are plucked. Midwives claim that an immense blood discharge is stopped by drinking goat urine, and if the dung is applied. The membrane of goats, aged in water after birth and taken as a drink in wine, expels the afterbirth. They consider it useful to fumigate the womb with the hair of kids. And in a discharge of blood, to drink the rennet or apply it with henbane seed. If the loins of a woman are rubbed with the blood of a black wild bull, Aeschines says that a weariness of sexual desire occurs. The same man says that goat urine mixed with nard is a drink for love, because of its potency. For infants, nothing is more useful than butter, by itself and with honey, both generally and for teething, and for the gums, and for mouth ulcers. A wolf's tooth tied on prevents the terrors of infants and diseases of teething. A wolf's skin does the same. Their largest teeth, when tied on, are said to provide an untiring run even for horses. The bowels of infants are stopped by applying hare rennet to the breast. Donkey liver, with a little all-heal <note>original: "panacea"</note> mixed in and instilled into the mouth, protects infants from the falling sickness <note>original: "comitialibus morbis"</note> and other diseases. They instruct that this be done for forty days. And an ass's skin thrown over them makes infants fearless. The teeth that first fall out from horses provide easy teething for infants when tied on. It is more effective if they have not touched the ground. Bull spleen is eaten in honey. It is also applied to pains of the spleen. For running ulcers, use it with honey. Calf spleen, boiled in wine, triturated, and applied, is for small mouth ulcers. Goat brain, passed through a gold ring, is instilled into infants before they are given milk, to prevent the falling sickness and other diseases of infants. Tied on with a cloth, goat dung keeps restless infants quiet, especially girls. Gums rubbed with goat's milk or hare's brain make teething easy. Cato believes that sleep is induced if hare is taken in food. The common people also believe it grants grace to the body for nine days, in a trivial way. Yet there must be some cause for such a strong persuasion. The magi say that sleep is induced by the bile of a sacrificed goat, applied to the eyes or placed under the pillow. Goat horn ash in myrtle oil, when rubbed on, inhibits sweat. Boar bile, when applied, stimulates intercourse. Likewise, drinking pig marrow. Ass's tallow mixed with the fat of a male goose, when applied. Likewise, the horse's act for Virgil <note>a reference to the classical belief in the aphrodisiacal properties of "hippomanes"</note>

<summary>This page covers various gynecological and pediatric medicinal recipes using animal products, such as hare, goat, donkey, and bull parts, to treat infertility, labor, and infant illnesses.</summary>
<keywords>womb, conception, infants, teething, labor, medical remedies, Pliny the Elder</keywords>

of roads and circles placed in such a way that those watching at a certain time see them clearly. Thus, ships, even if they go with full sails, still seem to stand still. There will be one who will demonstrate at some point in which parts the comets wander. Since they go so removed from the others, how great and of what kind they are. We are content with what has been discovered; let those who come after contribute something to the truth. Through the stars, he says, we do not see what lies further; through comets, we send our gaze across. First, if this happens, it does not happen in that part where the star itself is, of thick and solid fire, but where a rare splendor runs out and is scattered into hair. You see through the intervals of the fires, not through the fires themselves. All the stars, he says, are round; comets are elongated, from which it appears they are not stars. For who would concede to you that comets are long, the nature of which, like the others, is a sphere? But the brightness is extended just as the sun sends its rays far and wide. The form of the thing itself is one thing, and the light that flows from it is another. Thus, the body of the comets themselves is rounded. The splendor, however, appears longer than that of the other stars. Why, you ask? Tell me first, why does the moon receive a light very unlike the sun, when it receives it from the sun? Why does it now redden, now pale? Why is its color livid and black when it is excluded from the view of the sun? Tell me why all stars have a face in some way unlike each other, and most diverse from the sun. How does nothing prevent them from being stars, even if they are not similar, just as nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same lot as the others, even if they do not have a similar face? Furthermore, if you consider the world itself, is it not composed of diverse things? Why is it that in Leo the sun always burns and scorches the lands with heat? In Aquarius, it binds the winter and locks the rivers with ice? And yet, this star and that one are of the same condition <margin>† arises</margin> even though it is dissimilar in effect and nature. Within a very short time, Aries <margin>† is cultivated</margin>, Libra sets most slowly, and yet this star and that one are of the same nature, even though one ascends in a small amount of time and the other is brought forth for a long time. Do you not see how contrary the elements are among themselves? There are heavy and light, cold and hot, moist and dry. The whole harmony of this world consists of discord. You deny that a comet is a star because its form does not correspond to the model, nor is it similar to the others. For you see, that one which returns to its place in the thirtieth year is very similar to this one which revisits its seat within a year. Nature does not provide its work for one form, but boasts in variety itself. It made some things more sluggish, others swifter than others. It made some stronger, others more temperate, but some it led out from the crowd so that they might proceed individually and conspicuously, and some it sent into the flock. He is ignorant of the power of nature who does not think it is allowed to do anything except what it does more frequently. It does not show comets often; it assigns them another place, other times, motions unlike the others. It wanted to cultivate the magnitude of its work from these, whose face is more beautiful than you would think is accidental, whether you consider their amplitude or their splendor, which is greater and more ardent than that of the others. Indeed, it has a certain distinguished and singular face, not cast and tightened into a narrow space, but let out more freely, and embracing the region of many stars. Aristotle says that comets signify a storm and intemperance of winds and rains. What then? Do you not judge it to be a star that announces future things? For this is not a sign of a storm in the same way that oil sparking or rotten mushrooms growing is a sign of future rain, or how it is an indication of a raging sea if marine coots play on dry land and desert known marshes, and a heron flies above a high cloud. But it is so, just as the equinox is a sign of a year turning into heat and cold. Just as those things which the Chaldeans sing of, what a star determines for those born, whether sad or happy. So that you may know this is so, a comet’s rising does not immediately threaten winds and rains, as Aristotle says, but <margin>The rising of a comet makes the whole year suspect.</margin> it makes the whole year suspect. From which it appears that it did not draw the signs it gives for the near future from the near future, but has them stored and compressed by the laws of the world. That comet, which appeared when Patriculus and Vopiscus were consuls, did those things which were predicted by Aristotle and Theophrastus. For there were great and continuous storms everywhere. But in Achaia and Macedonia, cities were overthrown by earthquakes. Their slowness, he says, is an argument that they are heavier, and have much earthy matter in them. Their courses, moreover, are almost forced toward the cardinal points. Both are false. I will speak about the former first, because those things which are carried more slowly are heavy. What then? Is the star of Saturn, which completes its journey more slowly than all others, heavy? And yet it has an argument of lightness, in that it is above the others. But, you say, it travels in a larger

<summary>Seneca defends the celestial nature of comets against Aristotelian objections, arguing that their irregular forms and long-term effects do not disqualify them from being stars, and challenging the idea that slow movement implies greater density or terrestrial weight.</summary>
<keywords>Comets, Aristotle, Celestial Motion, Stoic Philosophy, Astronomy, Astrology, Elements</keywords>

And so, we saw the plundered and ruined foreign nations carried in a triumph over Massilia <note>Marseille</note>, and a triumph celebrated over that very city, without which our commanders never celebrated triumphs for wars beyond the Alps. I could recount many other nefarious deeds against our allies, if he had not seen something even more shameful in this one instance alone. We are punished justly, therefore. For if we had not tolerated their unpunished crimes, such license would never have reached one man. From him, the inheritance of private wealth came to a few, and the inheritance of corrupt desires came to the many. Nor, indeed, will the seed and cause of civil wars ever be lacking as long as ruined men remember that bloody spear and hope for it. When Lucius Sulla had brandished it while his kinsman was dictator, thirty-six years later, it did not depart from a more wicked man. Another man, who had been a scribe during that dictatorship, was city quaestor in this one. From this, it ought to be understood that, with such rewards proposed, civil wars will never be lacking. And so, the walls of the city merely stand and remain, and they themselves now fear the ultimate crimes. But the Republic itself, we have lost entirely. And we have fallen into these disasters, for we must return to the point, while we preferred to be feared rather than to be dear and loved. Third article: whether the more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third point, it proceeds thus. It seems that the more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because those things which are prior and better known by nature are posterior and less known to us. But universals are prior by nature because that from which the consequence of existing does not convert is prior; therefore, universals are posterior in the cognition of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior in relation to us than simple ones. But universals are simpler; therefore, they are later known in relation to us. Furthermore, the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition. But the more universal things are parts of the definition of the less universal; for instance, animal is a part of the definition of man; therefore, universals are later known in relation to us. Furthermore, we arrive at causes and principles through effects. But universals are certain principles; therefore, universals are later known in relation to us. But against this is what is said in the first book of the *Physics*: that from universals it is necessary to arrive at singulars. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive cognition. And because sense is of singulars, while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior in relation to us than the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. Now, everything that proceeds from potency to act arrives at the incomplete act, which is intermediate between potency and act, before it arrives at the perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; but the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known in a qualified sense in act, and in a way in potency. Hence the philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics* that those things that are first manifest and certain to us are more confused; later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each one of those things contained within it is to know something under a certain confusion. Yet in this way, both the universal whole in which the parts are contained in potency and the integral whole can be known; for either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the universal whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing; just as to know animal indistinctly is to know animal insofar as it is animal. But to know animal distinctly is to know animal insofar as it is rational or irrational, which is to know man or lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect to know animal before it knows man. And the same reasoning holds if we compare any more universal thing to a less universal thing. And because sense departs from potency into act just as the intellect does, the same order of <column-break/>cognition appears in the sense. For we judge the more common before the less common according to the sense, and according to both place and time. According to place, indeed, as when something is seen from a distance: it is first grasped as being a body before it is grasped as being an animal, and it is first grasped as being an animal before it is grasped as being a man, and first a man before Socrates or Plato. According to time, because a child from the beginning distinguishes man from non-man before he distinguishes this man from another man. And for this reason, children at the beginning call all men fathers. Later, however, they determine each one, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*. And the reason for this is manifest: because he who knows something indistinctly is still in potency to know the principle of distinction, just as he who knows the genus is in potency to know the difference. And thus it is clear that indistinct cognition is intermediate between potency and act. Therefore, it must be said that the cognition of singulars is prior in relation to us than the cognition of universals, just as sensitive cognition is prior to intellectual cognition. But both according to the sense and according to the intellect, the cognition of the more common is prior to the cognition of the less common. To the first, therefore, it must be said that the universal can be considered in two ways. In one way, according to the fact that the universal nature is considered simultaneously with the intention of universality. And since the intention of universality—namely, that one and the same thing has a relation to many—proceeds from the abstraction of the intellect, it is necessary that in this way the universal be posterior. Hence, in the first book *On the Soul*, it is said that the universal animal is either nothing or is posterior. But according to Plato, who posited subsistent universals, according to this consideration, the universal would be prior because particulars, according to him, are nothing but by participation in the subsistent universals which are called ideas. In another way, it can be considered regarding the nature itself, namely of animality or humanity as it is found in particulars. And thus it must be said that there is a twofold order of nature. One is according to the path of generation and time, according to which path those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the more common is prior according to nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For animal is generated before man, as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior according to nature than potency, and the perfect is prior to the imperfect; and in this way, the less common is prior according to nature than the more common, such as man than animal. For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of the animal, but intends to generate man. To the second, it must be said that the more common universal is compared to the less common as a whole and as a part: as a whole, indeed, according to which not only the less universal is contained in potency in the more universal, but also others; as under animal, not only man but also horse is contained. As a part, however, according to which the less common contains in its definition not only the more common but also others, as man [contains] not only animal but also rational. Thus, therefore, animal considered in itself is prior in our cognition than man. But man is prior in our cognition than [the fact] that animal is a part of his reason. To the third, it must be said that some part can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself; and thus nothing prevents one from knowing the parts before the whole, such as stones before a house. In another way, according to the fact that they are parts of this whole; and thus it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know a house by a certain confused cognition before we distinguish its individual parts. Thus, therefore, it must be said that those things which define are to be considered absolutely as known before the defined; otherwise, the defined would not be made known through them. *To correct is to take the corrected.* If one is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who has punished him lasts.
